Senses.Note: Four direct uses from four works establish a diagnostic against dividing one matter into disconnected halves.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: Puji Yulin: the book and 小參 section assign the exact instruction to Puji Yulin.

Occurrences.Kwic: 傅大士打作兩橛，剝也剝不開；山僧紐作一團，摶也摶不攏。

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問眾：「黃檗大師云：『不道無禪，只是無師。』黃檗與麼道，打作兩橛。

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: Yuan’an Feng: the own-record 師問眾 frame assigns the exact appraisal to Yuan’an Feng.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若離說底別覓無說則打作兩橛落斷常之見
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (M/M59/M59n1540.xml). General Discourses of Chan Master Dahui Pujue. Dahui Zonggao says seeking the unsaid apart from speech splits the matter into two pieces and falls into eternalism or annihilationism.

Senses.Explanation: To split it into two pieces is to treat one continuous matter as two disconnected realities. Chan masters use the carpentry image to expose divisions such as movement versus stillness, speech versus silence, or paired lines treated as separate truths. Puji Yulin says dividing movement and stillness shows that awakening is still lacking. Chaozong says Fu Dashi splits a verse while he himself twists it into one bundle. Yuan’an Feng applies the verdict to Huangbo’s assertion that there is Chan but no teacher. Dahui Zonggao says seeking the unsaid apart from speech creates two pieces and falls into eternalism or annihilationism.
